lessons.title: L1 · What Probability Really Means — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: A probability value is always a number that sits…
questions.correctFeedback: 0 means never, 1 means certain, and everything possible lives in between.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It runs from 0 (never) to 1 (certain). Percentages like 70% are just 0.7 in disguise.

questions.stem: The "bag of every possible outcome" is properly called the…
questions.correctFeedback: The sample space is the full collection of everything that could happen — the whole bag.
questions.incorrectFeedback: That's the sample space. An outcome is one item in the bag; an event is a chosen group of them.

questions.stem: "The die shows an even number" is best described as an…
options: event — a yes/no question on outcomes
outcome — one single face, like four
sample space — all six faces together
axiom — a basic rule we agree
questions.correctFeedback: It's an event: a chosen bunch of outcomes ({2,4,6}) that answers a yes/no question.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It's an event — a group of outcomes ({2,4,6}). A single outcome would be just one face, like 'a 4'.

questions.stem: If the chance a train is late is 0.2, the chance it is on time is…
options: zero point two, the same value
one point two, by adding one
zero point five, a coin toss
zero point eight, one minus it
questions.correctFeedback: Late and on-time can't both happen and cover everything, so on-time = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8 (the complement rule).
questions.incorrectFeedback: On-time = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8. 'Late' and 'on time' are opposites that together must total 1.

questions.stem: In the expression P(B | A), the vertical bar is read as the word…
options: divided, so the bar means a ratio
and, so both events must happen together
given, so A is already known true
or, so either one event may happen
questions.correctFeedback: The bar means "given". P(B|A) is the chance of B once you already know A happened.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It reads as "given". A division does appear in the formula, but the bar itself is not the division sign.

questions.stem: From Lesson 1: two fair dice are rolled. The chance that at least one shows a six is…
options: eleven over thirty-six, by the complement
two over six, one per die
one over thirty-six, both showing six
ten over thirty-six, minus both sixes
questions.correctFeedback: Right — no six on either die is 5 × 5 = 25 of 36 pairs, so at least one six is 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the complement: no six anywhere is 25 of the 36 pairs, so 1 − 25/36 = 11/36. Adding 1/6 + 1/6 counts the pair 6-6 twice.

questions.stem: A bag holds 5 white and 3 green balls. Two are drawn without replacement. P(both white) is…
options: five over eight times five over eight
five over eight plus four over seven
five over eight times three over eight
five over eight times four over seven
questions.correctFeedback: Right — (5/8) × (4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14. The second factor is conditional: one white is already gone.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B|A). First draw 5/8; then 7 balls remain with 4 white, so (5/8) × (4/7) = 5/14.

questions.stem: Two events A and B each have probability above zero and cannot both occur. They are…
options: independent, since one rules out other
not independent, since one rules other
independent only if P(A) equals P(B)
independent whenever P(A) exceeds one half
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Mutually exclusive means P(A ∩ B) = 0, but independence needs P(A)P(B), which is above zero. So they cannot be independent.
questions.incorrectFeedback: They are NOT independent. Learning A occurred tells you B certainly did not — that is maximal information, the opposite of independence.

lessons.title: L3 · Turning the Bar Around — Bayes' Theorem — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: For Bayes' theorem to apply, the causes B1…Bk must be…
options: independent of each other and equal
mutually exclusive and also jointly exhaustive
equally likely and also mutually independent
dependent on each other and disjoint
questions.correctFeedback: Right — they must form a partition: no two can co-occur, and together they cover every possibility.
questions.incorrectFeedback: They must be mutually exclusive AND exhaustive — a partition. They need not be equally likely, and independence is a different idea entirely.

questions.stem: In Bayes' theorem, the denominator is exactly the same thing as…
options: the prior probability of the cause
the largest of the branch weights
the likelihood of the observed data
the total probability of the effect
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the denominator is P(A), computed by the theorem of total probability as the sum of all branch weights.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It is P(A), the total probability of the effect: the sum of every branch weight. That is why the posterior is one branch's share of the total.

questions.stem: From Lesson 2: A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A ∩ B) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For independent events, multiply: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. Adding gives P(A or B) only for events that can't overlap.

questions.stem: A positive result on an accurate test for a rare disease often still means…
options: the test itself must have been faulty somehow
the disease is far more common than said
a low posterior, because the prior was low
a high posterior, because the test is good
questions.correctFeedback: Exactly — the healthy majority produce so many false alarms that they swamp the true positives. The base rate dominates.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The posterior stays low. With a rare disease, the huge healthy group generates far more false positives than the small sick group generates true ones.

lessons.title: L4 · From Events to Numbers — Random Variables — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: A random variable is best described as…
options: a number that changes whenever you look
the probability attached to every single outcome
a function from outcomes to real numbers
a set of outcomes sharing one property
questions.correctFeedback: Right — X(ω) takes an outcome and returns a number. Probability isn't part of the definition.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It's a function: outcome in, real number out. The probabilities belong to the sample space; the variable just carries them.

questions.stem: Three fair coin tosses, X = number of heads. P(X < 2) equals…
options: four over eight, the height before the jump
seven over eight, the height after the jump
three over eight, the jump size at two
one over eight, the height at zero heads
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — X < 2 means 0 or 1 heads: 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8. That's F(2−), the level just before the jump at 2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: X < 2 means 0 or 1 heads, so 1/8 + 3/8 = 4/8 — the level just before the jump. F(2) = 7/8 would be P(X ≤ 2).

questions.stem: Which of these could NOT be a distribution function?
options: one that is flat, then jumps, then stays flat
one that rises smoothly from zero up to one
one that jumps at every integer up to 1
one that rises to 0.9, then dips to 0.8
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — a running total of probability can never go down. Any dip breaks the non-decreasing property.
questions.incorrectFeedback: A d.f. may jump or rise smoothly, but it can never decrease. The one that dips from 0.9 to 0.8 is invalid.

questions.stem: From Lesson 2: events A and B each have positive probability and cannot occur together. Then A and B are…
options: independent, since they share no outcomes
dependent, since one excludes the other
independent, if both their probabilities match
dependent, only if they are exhaustive
questions.correctFeedback: Right — P(A∩B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0, so the product rule fails. Knowing A happened tells you B didn't.
questions.incorrectFeedback: They're dependent: P(A∩B) = 0 while P(A)P(B) > 0. Mutually exclusive is the opposite of independent here, not the same thing.

lessons.title: L5 · Mass and Density — Discrete vs Continuous — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: X is continuous with density f. Which statement is always true?
options: f(x) is never larger than one
F jumps exactly where f peaks
questions.correctFeedback: Right — a single point holds no probability for a continuous variable; probability lives on stretches.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For a continuous X, every single point has probability 0. A density can exceed 1, and its height is never itself a probability.

questions.stem: A discrete X has F(2) = 0.7 and F(2−) = 0.4. Then P(X = 2) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — mass at a point is the jump: F(2) − F(2−) = 0.3.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Mass at a point is the jump size: F(2) − F(2−) = 0.7 − 0.4 = 0.3.

questions.stem: X is uniform on (0, 1/4). What is its density on that stretch?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — height × width = 1 with width 1/4 forces height 4. Densities above 1 are fine.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The area must be 1 and the width is 1/4, so the height is 4. A density may exceed 1; only areas are probabilities.

questions.stem: From Lesson 4: for a discrete X, which pair can give different answers?
options: P(X ≤ a) and plain F(a) itself
questions.correctFeedback: Right — they differ by the jump at a, P(X = a). For a continuous X the jump is 0 and they agree.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The other pairs are identities. P(X < a) and P(X ≤ a) differ by the jump at a, which is P(X = a).

questions.stem: Which function could be a probability density?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — 2x is never negative on (0, 1) and its area is 1. The others have area 3, dip below 0, or have area 1/2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: 2x on (0, 1) has area 1 and is never negative. 3 has area 3; x − 1 is negative on (0, 1); 1/2 has area 1/2.

lessons.title: L6 · Expectation — the Balance Point — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: E[X] = 4. What is E[3X − 2]?
questions.correctFeedback: Right — linearity: 3 × 4 − 2 = 10.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Scale the balance point, then shift it: E[3X − 2] = 3E[X] − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10.

questions.stem: For any X that has a mean and E[X²], which is always true?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the gap E[X²] − (E[X])² is an average of squared distances from the mean, so it can't be negative.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X²] − (E[X])² is the average squared distance from the mean, never negative. So E[X²] ≥ (E[X])². (And the mean of a die, 3.5, is not a possible roll.)

questions.stem: X is the score on one roll of a fair die. E[X] is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — (1 + 2 + … + 6)/6 = 3.5. The mean need not be a value X can take.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X] = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.5. It's a balance point, not a face; nothing is rounded.

questions.stem: From Lesson 5: X is uniform on (0, 1/5). What is its density there?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — height × width must be 1, and the width is 1/5, so the height is 5.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The area under the density must be 1. Width 1/5 forces height 5. Densities may exceed 1; only areas are probabilities.

questions.stem: X has density 2x on (0, 1). Where does it balance?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — ∫ x · 2x dx from 0 to 1 = 2/3. More sand near 1 pulls the balance right of 1/2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X] = ∫₀¹ x · 2x dx = [2x³/3]₀¹ = 2/3. The sand piles up toward 1, so the balance sits right of the midpoint, but not at the peak.

lessons.title: L7 · Variance and Chebyshev — How Spread Out? — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: E[X] = 2 and E[X²] = 13. What is Var(X)?
questions.correctFeedback: Right — mean of the square minus square of the mean: 13 − 2² = 9.

questions.stem: Var(X) = 4. What is Var(−2X + 5)?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the shift drops out and the factor comes out squared: (−2)² × 4 = 16.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X). The 5 drops out; (−2)² = 4, so 4 × 4 = 16. A variance is never negative.

questions.stem: What does Chebyshev's inequality need to hold?
options: a normal, bell-shaped distribution of X
a symmetric distribution around its mean
a large sample of observed values
only a finite mean and variance
questions.correctFeedback: Right — it works for every shape, which is exactly why it's loose.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Chebyshev needs only a finite mean and variance. No normality, no symmetry, no sample size.

questions.stem: Mean 20, variance 16, shape unknown. A lower bound for P(12 < X < 28) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — σ = 4, so 8 = 2σ and the bound is 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

questions.stem: From Lesson 6: for a fair die, how does E[X²] compare with (3.5)²?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — E[X²] = 91/6 ≈ 15.17 > 12.25. The gap is the die's variance, 35/12.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The average of the squares always beats the square of the average unless X never varies: 91/6 ≈ 15.17 > 12.25.

lessons.title: L8 · Bernoulli and Binomial — Counting Successes — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: A binomial X has mean 4 and variance 3.2. What is n?
questions.incorrectFeedback: Divide: q = npq/np = 3.2/4 = 0.8. Then p = 0.2 and n = np/p = 4/0.2 = 20.

questions.stem: Which count is binomial?
options: tosses needed to get the first head
aces among 5 cards dealt without replacing
heads in 10 tosses of one coin
rainy days in a year of weather
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — fixed n = 10, independent tosses, same p, counting heads: BINS.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Only heads in 10 tosses passes BINS. Tosses-until-a-head has no fixed n; cards without replacement aren't independent; rainy days don't share one p and aren't independent.

questions.stem: Someone claims a binomial with mean 3 and variance 4. This is…
options: fine, whenever n is large enough
impossible, since variance exceeds the mean
questions.correctFeedback: Right — q = 4/3 would exceed 1. A binomial's variance npq is always below its mean np.
questions.incorrectFeedback: q = variance/mean = 4/3 > 1, which no probability can be. A binomial always has variance below its mean.

questions.stem: From Lesson 7: Var(X) = 3. What is Var(3 − X)?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the shift 3 drops out and (−1)² = 1, so the variance stays 3.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Var(a + bX) = b²Var(X). Here b = −1, so (−1)² × 3 = 3. A variance is never negative.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled 4 times. P(at least one six) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — the complement of 'at least one six' is 'no sixes', with chance (5/6)⁴.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the complement: P(no six in 4) = (5/6)⁴, so P(at least one) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518. Adding 1/6 four times double-counts.

lessons.title: L9 · Poisson — Counting Rare Events — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: Calls arrive at 6 per hour. What is λ for a 20-minute window?
questions.correctFeedback: Right — rate × length: 6 × 1/3 = 2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: λ scales with the window: 6 per hour × (20/60) hour = 2.

questions.stem: X is Poisson with variance 3. What is E[X²]?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — mean = variance = 3, and E[X²] = Var + mean² = 3 + 9 = 12.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For a Poisson the mean equals the variance, 3. Then E[X²] = Var(X) + (E[X])² = 3 + 9 = 12 (L7's shortcut, rearranged).

questions.stem: When is Poisson(np) a good stand-in for Bin(n, p)?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — many trials, each rare. The variances npq and np then nearly agree.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It needs many trials and a small chance each: n large, p small. Then npq ≈ np, as for a Poisson.

questions.stem: From Lesson 8: a binomial has mean 6 and variance 4.2. What is p?
questions.incorrectFeedback: Divide variance by mean: q = npq/np = 4.2/6 = 0.7, so p = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.

questions.stem: X is Poisson(λ). P(X ≥ 1) equals…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the complement of 'at least one' is 'none', with chance e^(−λ).
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the complement: P(X = 0) = e^(−λ), so P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − e^(−λ). λe^(−λ) is P(X = 1) alone.

lessons.title: L10 · Geometric and Negative Binomial — Waiting for Success — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: Each try succeeds with chance 1/4. X = tries until the first success. E[X] is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — 1/p = 4 tries on average.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X] = 1/p = 4 (counting trials). Counting failures before the success gives q/p = 3, so check the support.

questions.stem: No six in the first 10 rolls of a fair die. The chance of a six on roll 11 is…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — each roll is independent; the geometric wait is memoryless.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The die has no memory: given 10 misses, the next roll is still a six with chance 1/6. 'Due' is the gambler's fallacy.

questions.stem: Y = failures before the first success, with p = 1/5. E[Y] is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — failures convention: q/p = (4/5)/(1/5) = 4, one less than the 5 trials.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Failures before the first success: E[Y] = q/p = 4. The trials count X = Y + 1 has mean 5.

questions.stem: A fair coin. The chance the 2nd head comes on the 3rd toss is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — toss 3 is a head and the first 2 hold exactly one head: C(2, 1)(1/2)³ = 2/8 = 1/4.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The last toss must be the 2nd head, and the first two tosses hold exactly one head (2 patterns): 2 × (1/2)³ = 1/4.

questions.stem: From Lesson 9: typos occur at 1 per 4 pages. What is λ for a 12-page document?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — rate × window: (1/4) × 12 = 3.
questions.incorrectFeedback: λ is the rate times the window's length: 1/4 per page × 12 pages = 3.

lessons.title: L11 · Moment Generating Functions — a Barcode for a Distribution — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: M(t) = (0.3 + 0.7e^t)^10 is the MGF of…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — the barcode is (q + pe^t)^n, so p goes with e^t: p = 0.7, n = 10.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Match (q + pe^t)^n: the number beside e^t is p = 0.7, the other is q = 0.3, and the power is n = 10.

questions.stem: M(t) = e^(4(e^t − 1)). What is Var(X)?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — that's the Poisson(4) barcode, and a Poisson's variance equals λ.
questions.incorrectFeedback: e^(λ(e^t − 1)) is Poisson(λ); here λ = 4, and Var = λ = 4.

questions.stem: X ~ Bin(5, p) and Y ~ Bin(7, p) are independent. X + Y is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — (q + pe^t)^5 × (q + pe^t)^7 = (q + pe^t)^12.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Multiply the MGFs: (q + pe^t)^5(q + pe^t)^7 = (q + pe^t)^12, the Bin(12, p) barcode.

questions.stem: Which rule needs X and Y to be independent?
questions.correctFeedback: Right — E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always holds; M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y needs independence.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Linearity of means never needs independence (L6). The product rule for MGFs does: with Y = X it fails.

questions.stem: From Lesson 10: each try succeeds with chance 1/3. P(no success in the first 2 tries) is…
questions.incorrectFeedback: Both tries must fail: q² = (2/3)² = 4/9. 1/9 is both succeeding.

lessons.title: L12 · Uniform and Exponential — Flat Chances and Forgetful Waits — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: T is exponential with mean 4 minutes. Its rate λ is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — rate = 1/mean = 1/4 per minute.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For the exponential, the rate is 1 over the mean: 1/4 per minute. A rate of 4 per minute would mean a 15-second average wait.

questions.stem: T is exponential and P(T > 5) = 0.6. What is P(T > 8 | T > 3)?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — memoryless: given 3 survived, needing 5 more has chance P(T > 5) = 0.6.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Memorylessness: P(T > 3 + 5 | T > 3) = P(T > 5) = 0.6. The 3 units already survived don't count.

questions.stem: Buses arrive Poisson-style at 4 per hour. P(waiting more than 15 minutes) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — 15 minutes expects 4 × 1/4 = 1 bus, and an empty window has chance e^(−1).
questions.incorrectFeedback: Waiting more than 15 minutes means no bus in a quarter hour, where λ = 4 × 1/4 = 1. So the chance is e^(−1) ≈ 0.37.

questions.stem: X ~ U(2, 8). What is Var(X)?
From Lesson 10: which discrete distribution is memoryless?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the geometric; today's exponential is its continuous twin.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The geometric wait is the discrete memoryless one: P(X > m + k | X > m) = P(X > k). The exponential is its continuous twin.

lessons.title: L13 · The Normal Distribution — One Bell, Shifted and Stretched — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: X ~ N(50, 16). The z-score of 58 is…
questions.incorrectFeedback: Divide by the SD, not the variance: σ = √16 = 4, so z = 8/4 = 2.

questions.stem: X and Y are independent, Var(X) = 9 and Var(Y) = 16. The SD of X − Y is…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the variances add: 9 + 16 = 25, so the SD is 5.
questions.incorrectFeedback: For independent variables the variances add even for a difference: Var(X − Y) = 25, SD = 5.

questions.stem: For any normal, P(μ − 2σ < X < μ + 2σ) is about…
questions.incorrectFeedback: Within 2 SDs a normal holds about 95% (0.9545). 75% is only Chebyshev's guarantee for any shape.

questions.stem: From Lesson 7: for any distribution at all, the share within 2σ of the mean is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — Chebyshev: at least 1 − 1/2² = 3/4. The normal's 95% is far above that floor.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Chebyshev guarantees at least 1 − 1/k² = 3/4 within 2σ, for every shape. 95% is the normal's own figure.

questions.stem: X₁, X₂ are independent copies of X ~ N(μ, σ²). Which has the larger variance?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — Var(2X) = 4σ², but Var(X₁ + X₂) = σ² + σ² = 2σ².
questions.incorrectFeedback: Var(2X) = 2²σ² = 4σ², while independent copies add their variances: Var(X₁ + X₂) = 2σ². Same mean, different spread.

lessons.title: L14 · Gamma, Beta and Chi-square — One Family — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: χ²₁₀ has mean and variance…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — χ²ₙ has mean n and variance 2n.
questions.incorrectFeedback: χ²ₙ = Gamma(n/2, rate ½): mean n = 10, variance 2n = 20.

questions.stem: Events arrive Poisson at rate 2. T = time to the 3rd event. P(T > 1) equals…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the 3rd event is still to come after 1 exactly when at most 2 events fell in [0, 1], a Poisson(2) count.
questions.incorrectFeedback: T > 1 means fewer than 3 events by time 1. That count is Poisson(λt) = Poisson(2), so P(T > 1) = P(Poisson(2) ≤ 2).

questions.stem: T has density proportional to t³e^(−2t). What is E[T]?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — shape 4 (t to the power 4 − 1) and rate 2: mean 4/2 = 2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: t³ means shape 4; e^(−2t) means rate 2. Mean = shape/rate = 4/2 = 2.

questions.stem: From Lesson 12: T is exponential with mean 5. P(T > 10) is…
X ~ Beta(2, 3). E[X] is…
questions.incorrectFeedback: The beta's mean is a/(a + b) = 2/(2 + 3) = 0.4.

lessons.title: L15 · Joint, Marginal and Conditional — Two Variables at Once — UGC-NET 107

questions.correctFeedback: Right — add the Y = 1 cells over X: 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5.
questions.incorrectFeedback: A marginal adds the other variable out: P(Y = 1) = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5.

questions.stem: Same table. What is P(Y = 1 | X = 1)?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the X = 1 row is 0.1, 0.3, total 0.4; rescaled, 0.3/0.4 = 0.75.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Slice the X = 1 row (0.1 and 0.3, total 0.4) and rescale: 0.3/0.4 = 0.75.

questions.stem: f(x, y) = 4xy on the unit square. Are X and Y independent?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — rectangular support and f = (2x)(2y), each a density on (0, 1).
questions.incorrectFeedback: The support is a rectangle and f(x, y) = (2x)(2y), a product of a function of x and a function of y. So yes, independent.

questions.stem: From Lesson 3: P(A) = 0.01, P(+ | A) = 0.9, P(+ | not A) = 0.1. P(A | +) is closest to…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — 0.009/(0.009 + 0.099) ≈ 0.083. False positives from the large not-A group swamp the true ones.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Bayes: P(A | +) = 0.009/(0.009 + 0.099) ≈ 0.083, not 0.9. The rare condition's true positives are outnumbered.

questions.stem: (X, Y) is uniform on the triangle 0 < x < y < 1. Are X and Y independent?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — learning X = x forces Y > x, so the slices differ.
questions.incorrectFeedback: A constant density on a triangle is not a product: once X = x is known, Y must exceed x. Non-rectangular support rules independence out.

lessons.title: L16 · Transformations — the Distribution of g(X) — UGC-NET 107

questions.stem: X ~ U(0, 1). Y = −ln X has…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — P(−ln X ≤ y) = P(X ≥ e^(−y)) = 1 − e^(−y), the exponential with rate 1.
questions.incorrectFeedback: CDF method: −ln X ≤ y exactly when X ≥ e^(−y), so F_Y(y) = 1 − e^(−y): Exp(1).

questions.stem: X has density f and Y = 3X. Then f_Y(y) equals…
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — x = y/3 and |dx/dy| = 1/3: stretching by 3 thins the density by 3.
questions.incorrectFeedback: x = y/3, |dx/dy| = 1/3, so f_Y(y) = f(y/3)/3. Stretching the axis by 3 spreads the same probability three times thinner.

questions.stem: X ~ U(−1, 1) and Y = X². P(Y ≤ 1/4) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — Y ≤ 1/4 exactly when |X| ≤ 1/2, which has chance 1/2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Turn it into an event about X: X² ≤ 1/4 means −1/2 ≤ X ≤ 1/2, chance 1/2. Taking only x = √y would give 1/4.

questions.stem: From Lesson 14: χ²₂ is the same distribution as…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — χ²₂ = Gamma(1, rate 1/2), the exponential with mean 2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: χ²ₙ = Gamma(n/2, rate 1/2); with n = 2 the shape is 1, which is the exponential with rate 1/2, mean 2.

questions.stem: A solution writes f_Y(y) = f_X(g⁻¹(y)) for an increasing g. What is missing?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the squeeze factor |dx/dy| = |d g⁻¹(y)/dy|.
questions.incorrectFeedback: It forgets the squeeze factor: f_Y(y) = f_X(g⁻¹(y)) · |dx/dy|. Without it the 'density' need not even have area 1.
